name: Thiamine (vitamin B1)
short: Most cited safety data concern injections: anaphylaxis is rare but can be life-threatening (case reports). A small trial of high-dose oral thiamine reported only mild side effects.
text: Most of the cited safety evidence concerns thiamine given by injection rather than by mouth. A case report described anaphylaxis after intravenous thiamine and noted that, although felt to be uncommon, it can be life threatening and that cases had been reported with some regularity outside the US; the authors judged thiamine relatively safe given the large number of patients treated without side effects, but not completely innocuous. A review of sales and adverse incident data for one injectable thiamine-containing product in the UK found 10 reported anaphylactic reactions over roughly 5.4 to 6.7 million patient-days of treatment; the authors said the incidence was difficult to estimate because the number of doses given is unknown, and concluded that the risk is reasonably assumed to be low. In a retrospective chart review of 8606 undiluted intravenous push administrations in 2595 adults at one hospital, no anaphylactic or anaphylactoid reactions were observed and there were 26 injection site reactions (0.30%; phlebitis and infiltration). For thiamine taken by mouth, a randomised crossover trial of high-dose oral thiamine in 40 patients with inflammatory bowel disease reported only mild side effects; the abstract does not say what they were. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
